KEY MESSAGE 1...

The main course of hazards being served this Thanksgiving
holiday across the Central Appalachians will be strong wind
gusts forged by a coastal low pressure system. Local reporting
stations this afternoon have already indicated an uptick in
surface gusts to 20 to 30 mph along our higher mountain ridge
zones. Further intensification in low level easterly winds are
expected late this evening into Thursday, which remains on track
to mix down to the surface at times overnight into Thanksgiving.
Latest forecast saw little to no change from previous thinking
in regards to surface gust intensities, ranging from 25 to 35
mph across the lowlands and up to 55 to 60 mph along the 
mountains. Locally higher gusts are not out of the question, as 
forecast soundings suggest winds hovering just above the surface
will be near 60 to 70 mph at its peak Thursday morning, but
achieving such gusts will be difficult based on the moist
profile caused by moderate to heavy rain at the time.

With all of that in mind, wind headlines remain unchanged from
their initial issuance from the overnight forecast package. High
Wind Warnings will be in place late tonight into Thursday
evening for our higher mountain ridge zones and Wind Advisories
for surrounding counties across northeast West Virginia.


KEY MESSAGE 2...

In addition to strong winds, this vertically stacked system also
advertises the return of widespread precipitation beginning late
tonight. Mid to upper level clouds have already invaded the area
as of the time of writing, with further ceiling deterioration
expected this evening, alongside the start of showers from the
south. Rain chances increase in earnest from south to north
through the predawn hours, leading to a wet and gloomy
Thanksgiving holiday. Overall rain totals are forecast to remain
between half an inch to slightly over an inch in the area, which
should keep concerns of flooding at bay. However, exude caution
while traveling along the wet roadways as this will be the first
rainfall of significance in sometime.

Will also note there will be a brief and localized period of
freezing rain possible late this evening into early Thursday
morning for portions of Pocahontas and Randolph Counties that
could result in a light glaze of ice in time for any morning
holiday travel. Opted to join in on a Special Weather Statement
with the Sterling WFO to highlight this potential. Surface
and low level temperatures rise above freezing after daybreak
Thursday, allowing for an all rain regime to mask the region
during the day Thursday.

As the tail end of this powerful disturbance lifts northward,
the westward flank slides through the Ohio Valley to maintain
high end chance of POPs heading into Friday. Additionally, much
colder air will be drawn into the area overnight and will cause
precipitation to change over to a wintry mix just before dawn
Friday morning. While not expecting wintry impacts to the lower
elevations due to warm ground temperatures and melting
processes, attention will then turn to the mountains once more
as further transformation into snow is progged on Friday. Snow
showers will prevail into the conclusion of this departing
system, allotting to potential culmination of a few tenths of 
an inch to locally higher amounts by Saturday morning.

The surface low and its parent trough are expected to drift off
the New England coast overnight Friday into Saturday morning,
with some leftover snow showers lingering into the weekend along
the northeast mountains. Otherwise, precipitation in the lower
elevations will come to an end Friday night.


KEY MESSAGE 3...

Lingering upslope showers will come to an end Saturday morning,
with quieter weather set to begin the weekend. However, a
southern stream disturbance taking aim for the Ohio and
Tennessee Valleys is slated to track into the forecast area by
the second half of the day Sunday into the start of next week.
As it currently stands, mostly rain is expected to accompany
this system in response to above normal temperatures at the
onset of its arrival, but once again changing over to wintry
precipitation along the mountains during the overnight hours.
